items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-05-26
items.q: Sharky might because Sharky got up and Sharky lost his place in the jazz club by telling the people I was the one who brought this music around the world.

ctx.x: And he had some very nice things to say about you and talked about your playing. So you'll be happy to know that other people are backing your story up. If you go to the musicians, some of them will. And Raymond is one of them who will back you up.

Well, Sharky might because Sharky got up and Sharky lost his place in the jazz club by telling the people I was the one who brought this music around the world. Sharky was pulled off a program for the same thing. Now, Sharky was born about eight, nine years old when I was a musician playing music. Sharky wasn't playing music. Harry Shields wasn't playing music. Parenti wasn't playing music. George's Brunessons that they played. They weren't around. But they all got their mouth open big as an alligator trying to…
Now, I know you or I, we don't want to take credit away from Bix for what he had. Bix is a great man. Yes.

items.title: Sharkey Bonano Interview, 1966-11-09
items.q: La Rocca left and came back home and I was finished at Nix and they asked me would I join them and I joined them.

ctx.x: I'm sorry, most of all I missed Shields, the only chance I ever had to hear him. Then they got that Dixieland band together and traveled around the country and I just missed them in Memphis and I missed them down here about 1937. Yeah, I played with them. Yeah, you made some records then when La Rocca left.
La Rocca left and came back home and I was finished at Nix and they asked me would I join them and I joined them. Did you travel with them?

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-06-14
items.q: Even Sharky was imitating Paul Whiteman.

ctx.x: And they're saying there was some part of the creation of jazz. That Jack Lane, who played a drum and lousy drums at that, created jazz. Now that's good enough for men who thrive on thievery, on a word that we had nothing to do. Our jazz was started in Chicago. We took in the ragtime and changed the rhythm in Chicago. In 1916, we seen we were going to be a flop the first night. And I, being a good dancer, I watched those people. At that time, they had Vernon Castle doing the castle walk. And everybody was trying…

No, I wrote that mostly as a sort of, you might say, editor. Walter Allen managed to interview the various musicians that were still living. And he sent me the facts and I wrote them, sewed them up together. I was more concerned with the records than with the legends. I wasn't very interested in these obscure people from the shadows who were said to have played with this, that and the other musician, in this, that and the other band, and who never made any records at all. I'm not interested in music I can't hear…
